newsitem.title: ITALY: League cries victory on "vote to split Italy".
newsitem.headline: League cries victory on "vote to split Italy".

text.p: The Northern League party on Monday claimed to have won strong support for its drive for a separate state in northern Italy in a "referendum" it staged on the issue to howls of condemnation and derision from its opponents.

The party estimated on the basis of its own "exit polls" that some six million people out of a potential 22 million took part in Sunday's unofficial exercise across the north, with 99.7 percent saying "Yes" to an independent "Republic of Padania".
The figures, open to doubt after many journalists covering the event reported that they had voted several times at different locations, were impossible to verify.
They were taken with a large pinch of salt by mainstream political parties, which noted that the exercise had no juridical value and had not been open to independent scrutiny.

The League said it would announce the result of a full count later on Monday but party leader Umberto Bossi lost no time in crying victory. "Padania now exists...and it is leaving (Italy)," he told reporters late on Sunday.
Padania is the name Bossi has given to his nebulous state, a concept that exists only in the League's propaganda and has no recognised powers, institutions or borders.
Politicians across the mainstream spectrum have mocked what they call Bossi's "antics", including a much-publicised but poorly attended declaration of independence last September.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi on Sunday dismissed the referendum as a stunt and President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro cautioned that Italy had to remain "one and indivisible".

Derision of the League, however, has shifted to concern since eight separatist paramilitaries occupied the bell tower in the lagoon city of Venice this month to publicise a drive for an independent Venetian republic.
The eight, who went on trial last week, are not directly associated with the League but Bossi's opponents have argued that his secessionist rhetoric has incited hotheads.
Luigi Manconi, leader of the environmentalist Greens party in Prodi's colaition, said on Monday that while the referendum figures sounded bloated, the exercise itself should not be underestimated.
"The fact remains that this referendum has not failed in its aims and...that its shows a very strong demand coming from the people of those regions" for a federal system, he said.
The League has built support on genuine frustration with past political corruption in Italy and at stifling taxes and an inefficient, highly centralised bureaucracy.
It won around 10 percent of the national vote at general elections last year, though support has dropped since Bossi switched from a federalist to a separatist agenda.
The party has so far boycotted an all-party parliamentary commission on constitutional reform, whose brief includes drafting proposals for federal devolution, calling it a sham.
Senior League politician Roberto Maroni suggested in a radio interview on Monday that the party could continue to ignore the commission after Sunday's event.
"Yesterday's vote tells us that we have to move faster than we expected," Maroni said. "If they continue to play down this fact in Rome then they risk facing some nasty surprises."
He said that if there were doubts about the League's figures, then the Italian state should stage its own referendum.
